models_evaluated: Sepsis prediction score (six dichotomous variables, 0-6 points)

links.outcome: Referral rates and costs at different model cut-offs compared with usual care
links.effect: Observed referral cost €5890 per patient vs €5954-€6742 at model cut-offs; low cut-offs raised sepsis referral (99%, 91% vs 88%) but unnecessary referral rose to 85% and 56%; no cut-off saved costs.
links.quote: However, referral was also substantially higher for patients who did not need hospital assessment.

links.outcome: Cost per patient of model-guided referral versus usual GP care
links.effect: Model-based referral cost €5954-€6742 per patient vs €5890 observed; probabilistic analysis showed higher model costs than usual care in 83% of runs.
links.quote: In the probabilistic sensitivity analyses, costs for the prediction model were higher than usual care in 83% of the runs ( figure 3 ).

links.outcome: Whether model-guided referral improves outcomes or costs versus standard care
links.effect: Cost savings from referring sepsis patients were offset by unnecessary referral for all cut-offs; authors state improvement of care must be shown in an implementation study before guideline inclusion.
links.quote: The model should only be incorporated in sepsis guidelines for GPs if improvement of care can be demonstrated in an implementation study.

links.outcome: Referral and mortality effects of different risk cut-offs
links.effect: Low cut-offs (2, 3) increased unnecessary referrals (85%, 56% vs 15% observed); cut-off 4 lowered sepsis referral to 60% and raised estimated sepsis mortality (18 vs 9 cases).
links.quote: At higher prediction model cut-offs (scores 3 and 4), sepsis mortality will increase according to the expert opinion analysis.

links.outcome: Adequacy of model score as replacement for clinical judgement
links.effect: Authors conclude discrimination is insufficient to replace GP judgement; advise using score to estimate risk within overall judgement rather than strict cut-offs.
links.quote: Given the results of the current study, it can be concluded that the discrimination of our new sepsis score is not sufficient to replace the clinical judgement of the GP based on the results of this early economic evaluation.

unlisted_practices: Early health economic evaluation with decision-tree modelling of a predictive model before implementation
Expert panel estimation of the impact of referral changes on mortality and costs

links.outcome: Referral, mortality, and costs by cutoff
links.effect: Observed care cost €5890/patient; prediction-model cutoffs cost €5954–€6742; cutoff 4 sepsis referral was 60%.
links.quote: At a high cut-off score of 4, referral rates for patients who did not need hospital assessment were still higher than the observed referral rate, while at the same time referral in patients with sepsis who needed hospital assessment was lower (60%).

links.effect: Observed referral had the lowest average cost, €5890/patient; prediction-model scenarios ranged €5954–€6742/patient.
links.quote: The decision tree analysis shows that the observed probabilities of referral led to the lowest costs with average patient costs of €5890.

links.outcome: sepsis mortality under prediction model referral cut-offs
links.effect: Sepsis mortality was estimated at 12 cases at cut-off 3 and 18 cases at cut-off 4, compared with 9 observed cases under standard care.
links.quote: At higher prediction model cut-offs (scores 3 and 4), sepsis mortality will increase according to the expert opinion analysis.

links.outcome: average healthcare cost per patient compared with standard care
links.effect: Observed standard-of-care referral probabilities yielded the lowest average cost of €5890 per patient, while prediction model scenarios ranged from €5954 to €6742.
links.quote: The decision tree analysis shows that the observed probabilities of referral led to the lowest costs with average patient costs of €5890.
